x: Soap is the sodium or potassium salt of long-chain (C₁₂–C₁₈) fatty acids. Calcium and magnesium salts are the insoluble scum, and sulphonates are detergents.
t: Discriminate soap (carboxylate) from detergent (sulphonate).

x: Option D is incorrect: caustic soda (NaOH) gives hard soap, while soft soap uses caustic potash (KOH). The other statements are right.
t: Discriminate hard soap (NaOH) from soft soap (KOH).

x: Both are true and R explains A: Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ in hard water turn soap into insoluble scum, so it lathers poorly and cleans badly.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Sodium rosinate boosts lather, glycerol keeps shaving soap moist, sodium silicate adds hardness and sulphur fights acne, giving a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i.
t: Recall the role of each soap additive.

x: I, II and IV are correct: detergents' calcium and magnesium salts stay soluble, so they lather and clean in hard water. III is false because detergent solutions are usually neutral.
t: Discriminate soap (alkaline) from detergent (neutral).

x: Palmitic acid is C₁₅H₃₁COOH (16 carbons) and stearic acid C₁₇H₃₅COOH (18 carbons), giving a-ii, b-i.
t: Recall the carbon count of fatty acids.

x: The hydrocarbon chain is the water-hating tail that dissolves in grease, and –COO⁻Na⁺ is the water-loving head that dissolves in water, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the two ends of a soap molecule.

x: All three are correct: saponification is fat or oil reacting with alkali to give soap and glycerol.
t: Recall the products of saponification.

x: Both are true: soap is made from both vegetable and animal fats and oils.
t: Recall the raw materials of soap.

x: All six oils are used to make soap: peanut, mahua, castor, coconut, olive and palm kernel.
t: Recall the oils used in soap making.

x: All three are correct: soap tails bury themselves in grease to form micelles, which suspend it as tiny droplets that water rinses away.
t: Recall how micelles clean.

x: Both are true and R explains A: soap hydrolyses to give an alkaline solution, which harms delicate fibres such as silk and wool.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Hard water wastes soap, because much of it is used up forming scum before any lather appears.
t: Recall the effect of hard water on soap.

x: All three are correct: detergent surfactants can be ionic, non-ionic or zwitterionic, and alkylbenzene sulphonates and sodium lauryl sulphate are common detergents.
t: Recall the types of detergent.

x: Sodium lauryl sulphate is an anionic detergent with a 12-carbon chain, while detergents in general have 12–18 carbon chains and a sulphonate head, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii.
t: Recall the structure of detergents.

x: Both are true and R explains A: detergent solutions are near neutral, so they do not damage delicate fabrics.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Option C is incorrect: some older detergents with branched chains were non-biodegradable and caused foaming in rivers. Soap is biodegradable and harsh on delicate clothes.
t: Recall the biodegradability of soaps and detergents.

x: Alitame is about 2000 times sweeter than sucrose, the sweetest of these. Sucralose is about 600 times, saccharin about 550 and aspartame about 100.
t: Recall the sweetness ladder of artificial sweeteners.

x: Option C is incorrect: boric acid is an old preservative, no longer preferred because it is toxic. Sodium benzoate, propionates and metabisulphite are current preservatives.
t: Discriminate old from modern food preservatives.

x: Both are true and R explains A: antiseptics are gentle enough for living tissue, while disinfectants are too toxic and are used only on objects.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Aspirin is linked to willow bark, quinine comes from cinchona, morphine and codeine from opium and reserpine from Rauwolfia serpentina, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Recall the natural source of each drug.

x: I, II and III are correct: antipyretics lower fever, opioids relieve pain with sedation and addiction risk, and antibiotics act on bacteria but not viruses. IV is false because tranquillizers reduce anxiety.
t: Recall the action of each drug class.

x: Both are true: penicillin from the mould Penicillium notatum was the first antibiotic, and Waksman coined the word "antibiotic" in 1942.
t: Recall the history of antibiotics.

x: Chip packets are filled with nitrogen to push out oxygen, preventing the oil from going rancid and stopping microbes.
t: Recall why nitrogen is used in packaging.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: reversibility applies to all anaesthetics; the limited area and retained consciousness come from blocking only local nerves.
t: Check whether R explains the specific feature in A.

x: Sodium benzoate preserves soft drinks and juices, sorbates cheese and pickles, SO₂ dried fruit and wine, and propionates grains and cheese, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
t: Recall the use of each preservative.

x: Three are artificial sweeteners: aspartame, alitame and sucralose. Stevia comes from a plant and is a natural sweetener.
t: Discriminate natural from artificial sweeteners.

x: Sodium benzoate is C₇H₅NaO₂, benzoic acid with one H replaced by Na. C₇H₆O₂ is benzoic acid and Na₂S₂O₅ is metabisulphite.
t: Recall the formula of sodium benzoate.

x: Sorbates act against yeasts and moulds, sodium metabisulphite is Na₂S₂O₅, benzoic acid is used as its salts and formic acid has limited use, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-i, d-iv.
t: Recall the facts about each preservative.

x: Formic acid is listed as an antibacterial preservative. Fructose is a sugar and MSG a flavour enhancer.
t: Recall the role of each additive.

x: Both are true: vinegar is dilute acetic acid, and it preserves pickles and sauces by making them acidic.
t: Recall vinegar as a preservative.

x: Monosodium glutamate is MSG, sold as Ajinomoto. Stevia, saccharin and alitame are sweeteners.
t: Recall the trade name of MSG.

x: Both are true and R explains A: MSG gives the savoury umami taste, which is why it enhances flavour.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Besides enhancing flavour, MSG has a mild preservative action. It is not an antipyretic or a strong disinfectant.
t: Recall the roles of MSG.

x: All three are correct: fructose is the sweetest natural sugar, and invert sugar, a glucose–fructose mix, is sweeter than sucrose.
t: Recall the sweetness of natural sugars.

x: Both are true: a wax coating cuts water loss, and lower oxygen slows respiration and ripening, so produce keeps longer.
t: Recall the methods of preserving fruits and vegetables.

x: All four are correct: aspirin and paracetamol lower fever, and aspirin is a non-narcotic painkiller that does not affect consciousness.
t: Recall the action of aspirin and paracetamol.

x: Three are opioids: morphine, codeine and heroin. Paracetamol is a non-narcotic analgesic.
t: Discriminate narcotic from non-narcotic analgesics.

x: All four are correct: alcohol, iodine, H₂O₂, boric acid, KMnO₄ and iodoform are antiseptics, while phenol, chlorine, bleaching powder and formaldehyde are disinfectants.
t: Discriminate antiseptics from disinfectants.

x: Both are true: reserpine and barbiturates are tranquillizers, and Seconal and Luminal are barbiturates.
t: Recall the tranquillizers.

x: Chloramphenicol and sulphadiazine are both antibacterial drugs. The other pairs mix analgesics, antiseptics, disinfectants and tranquillizers.
t: Classify each drug by its action.

x: All four are correct: general anaesthesia causes unconsciousness, and sedatives calm and stop convulsions, potassium bromide being an old sedative.
t: Recall the action of anaesthetics and sedatives.

x: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928. Waksman coined the word "antibiotic" in 1942.
t: Discriminate Fleming (1928) from Waksman (1942).

x: All three are correct: reserpine is a tranquillizer that also lowers blood pressure, and quinine treats malaria.
t: Recall the uses of reserpine and quinine.

x: Hydrogen peroxide cleans wounds and kills germs, ethanol is both antiseptic and disinfectant, and boric acid is a mild antiseptic, giving a-iii, b-i, c-ii.
t: Recall the use of each antiseptic.

x: Iodine and iodoform are skin antiseptics, KMnO₄ and crystal violet are antiseptics and garlic has natural antiseptic power, giving a-ii, b-ii, c-iii, d-i, e-iii.
t: Recall the antiseptics and their uses.

x: All five are correct: phenol and methylphenol disinfect surfaces, chlorine and bleaching powder disinfect water and surfaces, and formaldehyde is strong.
t: Recall the disinfectants.

x: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928. 1942 is when Waksman coined "antibiotic".
t: Recall Fleming's 1928 discovery.

x: Fungi and bacteria are the main sources of antibiotics, and Streptomyces and Bacillus are key bacterial sources. Because List-II repeats in pairs, every code technically fits, so the key gives a-iv, b-ii, c-i, d-iii.
t: Recall that repeated List-II entries can make several codes fit.

x: I and II are correct: most antibiotics are natural or semi-synthetic, and some are fully synthetic. III is false because many come from bacteria, not only fungi.
t: Check each statement for the words "all" and "only".

x: Chloramphenicol is broad-spectrum, acting on many kinds of bacteria. Penicillin is narrower and reserpine is not an antibiotic.
t: Discriminate broad-spectrum from narrow-spectrum antibiotics.

x: Reserpine is a strong tranquillizer and an antihypertensive, and barbiturates reduce anxiety and induce sleep. Pairing in order gives a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall that the code pairs items in order when List-I repeats.

x: Sodium benzoate's food additive code is E211. C₇H₅NaO₂ is its formula, and soft drinks are where it is used.
t: Recall the E-code of sodium benzoate.
